docs.title: payforge
docs.text:
The billing runtime for a product whose pricing and packaging is described by a pricing spec. The spec says what is offered; payforge does what that needs at the payment provider, Stripe today: it computes the products and prices the provider should hold, starts checkout and the customer portal, verifies webhooks, and turns a paid subscription into an entitlement through ports the host supplies.

  • Overview: what it does and does not do, the packages, free mode.
  • The catalog: the spec as products and prices, found by lookup keys, and syncing.
  • Checkout and the portal: subscribing, buying once, managing a subscription.
  • Webhooks: verifying Stripe's events and what they carry.
  • The lifecycle: events to entitlements, and writing a store and a sink.
  • Marketplaces: sellers, sales with a platform fee, refunds.
  • Known limitations: what is not covered and what has not yet run against real Stripe.

Runnable examples cover a catalog sync, a pricing page, a webhook endpoint and limit checks.

go get github.com/plexusone/payforge

docs.title: payforge user guide
docs.text:
payforge is the billing runtime for a product whose pricing and packaging is described by a pricing spec. The spec says what is offered. payforge does what that needs at the payment provider, which is Stripe today:

  1. Catalog: the spec becomes products and prices in your Stripe account, found again by stable lookup keys.
  2. Checkout and the portal: a buyer is sent to a hosted page to subscribe or to buy something once, and to another to manage their subscription.
  3. Webhooks: Stripe's events are verified and reduced to a small set your code can rely on.
  4. The lifecycle: those events become an entitlement for the account, through a store and a sink you write.
  5. Marketplaces: sellers with their own Stripe accounts, sales with a platform fee, refunds.
  6. Known limitations: what is not covered and what has not yet run against real Stripe.

Runnable versions of the main pieces are in examples/.

docs.title: What payforge does not do
docs.text:
• It does not store anything. Your code keeps accounts, plans and processed events; payforge calls it through ports you supply.
  • It does not enforce limits. The spec answers "may this account add one more board?"; see examples/limits.
  • It does not talk to any provider but Stripe, though the core package knows nothing about Stripe and a second adapter could implement the same interfaces.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text: Package Holds github.com/plexusone/payforge The provider-neutral core: Billing, Connect, events, Lifecycle, the ports and in-memory versions of them github.com/plexusone/payforge/stripe The Stripe adapter: Client, Webhook, catalog sync github.com/plexusone/payforge/payforgetest Conformance suites to run against your own store and sinks

docs.title: A first run
docs.text:
Install and check a spec, with no Stripe account:

go run ./examples/catalog -spec examples/catalog/pricing.json

It prints the plans and products and says it is in free mode. Set STRIPE_SECRET_KEY to a test-mode key and the same command shows what syncing would create, without writing anything.

docs.title: Free mode
docs.text:
A host with no Stripe key is in free mode: every account is on the spec's default plan, and every operation that needs Stripe returns payforge.ErrNotConfigured. Use it for development and for deployments that do not sell anything:

var billing payforge.Billing = payforge.Disabled(spec)
if key != "" {
    billing, err = stripe.New(spec, stripe.Config{SecretKey: key})
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
}

Check the configuration once at startup, so a half-configured deployment stops instead of showing plans that never change:

err := payforge.CheckStartup(spec, payforge.ProviderConfig{
    SecretKey:      key,
    WebhookSecrets: []string{platformSecret, connectSecret},
})

With no key it succeeds. With a key it requires a valid spec, something to sell, and a webhook secret: two when the spec has a marketplace or a seller-set product, because events from sellers' accounts arrive on their own endpoint. Errors name what is missing and never contain a secret.

docs.title: The catalog
docs.text: The pricing spec is a JSON document. This page covers only what payforge reads; the format is described in the spec repository, and a complete example is examples/catalog/pricing.json.

docs.title: What becomes what
docs.text:
In the spec At Stripe A plan with prices One product, and one recurring price per interval A plan with no prices (free or arranged) Nothing: it is never sold through checkout A one-time product with an amountCents One product, and one price A seller-set product A product only; the amount is chosen at checkout

A plan is sold through checkout only if it is selfServe and has a price for the interval. An arranged plan such as Enterprise is set up by a person, not by a buyer.

docs.title: Lookup keys
docs.text:
Every price payforge creates carries a lookup key, and everything finds prices by it, never by Stripe's price ID:

  • A plan's price: <app>/<plan>/<interval>, for example taskboard/plus/month.
  • A product's price: <app>/<product>.

Product IDs are chosen by payforge too, as payforge_<app>_<plan>. Lookup keys are why one Stripe account can serve several products: each has its own app. Objects carry payforge_app, payforge_plan, payforge_product, payforge_subject and payforge_seller metadata, which is how an event is matched to the account it belongs to.

docs.title: Syncing
docs.text:
Prices must exist before anyone can check out, so sync the catalog to the account first. Always look before you write:

report, err := client.Sync(ctx, true) // true: a dry run, nothing is written
for _, a := range report.Actions {
    fmt.Println(a.Kind, a.Key, a.Detail)
}
if err != nil {
    return err // the report lists what happened before the failure
}
if report.Changed() {
    _, err = client.Sync(ctx, false)
}

The actions are create_product, update_product, create_price, replace_price and unchanged. Sync follows four rules:

  • It is safe to repeat. A second run changes nothing.
  • It never deletes. A product or price that is no longer in the spec stays at Stripe, so existing subscribers keep what they pay for.
  • It never edits an amount. Stripe prices are immutable. When the spec's amount, currency or interval changes, sync creates a new price, moves the lookup key to it and leaves the old price for the subscribers already on it.
  • It reports a failure with what happened before it. Run it again after fixing the cause.
  • It refuses what is not its own. A product at Stripe whose metadata names another app is stripe.ErrForeign, and an archived one is stripe.ErrArchived; un-archive it or choose another plan ID. A deleted product is stripe.ErrDeleted; its ID can never be used again, so the plan needs a new ID in the spec.

The command-line version is examples/catalog; it runs a dry run unless given -apply.

docs.title: Changing the catalog
docs.text:
You change What happens A plan's price A new price; subscribers stay on the old one until you move them A plan's name or features The product's name is updated; features live in the spec, not at Stripe A plan's ID A new product and new prices. The old ones stay; sync does not rename them, and existing subscribers keep their old price, which the spec no longer names. Avoid renaming plan IDs; add a new plan and retire the old one instead A plan removed from the spec Nothing at Stripe. A subscription on a price the spec does not know stops granting that plan

The last row is deliberate: only a price the spec has can grant a plan, so a price made by hand in the Stripe dashboard can never give anyone Enterprise. See the lifecycle.

docs.title: Accounts that already have objects
docs.text: If the Stripe account was used before payforge, subscriptions and customers exist with metadata of the host's own naming. Give the webhook reader and the lifecycle the prefix the host used (LegacyPrefixes: []string{"myapp"}) and myapp_organization_id and myapp_plan are read as the subject and the plan. A legacy subscription grants only a self-serve plan that has prices.

docs.title: Checkout and the customer portal
docs.text:
All three operations return a URL on a page hosted by Stripe. Send the buyer there; nothing about a card ever touches your server.

client, err := stripe.New(spec, stripe.Config{SecretKey: key})

stripe.Config takes the secret key, an optional HTTPClient, AllowedURLHosts and MaxNetworkRetries (default 2, and zero means the default, so retries cannot be turned off; they reuse the idempotency key). The key is never included in an error. A *stripe.Client implements payforge.Billing.

Give every call a context with a deadline. Without one a call can wait for the library's own timeout and its retries, which is minutes, and Sync makes many calls in a row.

docs.title: URLs
docs.text: Success, cancel, return and refresh URLs must be https (or http for localhost), and may not carry a user name or password. Set AllowedURLHosts to your own hostnames, and a URL that names any other host is refused with ErrInvalidURL. Do that whenever a URL is built from anything a user sent: without it, a buyer can be sent through a genuine Stripe checkout and land on a page of an attacker's choosing, holding the session ID.

docs.title: A subject
docs.text:
Everything is for a subject: the account in your system that pays, usually an organization.

subject := payforge.Subject{ID: org.ID, Name: org.Name, Email: org.BillingEmail}

ID is required: 1 to 128 letters, digits and . _ : -, starting with a letter or digit. Anything else is payforge.ErrInvalidSubject, because the ID is placed in search queries and idempotency keys. The first call for a subject creates a Stripe customer carrying the ID in metadata; later calls find it. client.EnsureCustomer(ctx, subject) does only that. You may keep the customer ID, but need not.

docs.title: Subscribing to a plan
docs.text:
sess, err := client.CheckoutPlan(ctx, payforge.PlanCheckout{
    Subject:    subject,
    Plan:       "plus",
    Interval:   pricingspec.IntervalMonth,
    SuccessURL: "https://app.example.com/billing",
    CancelURL:  "https://app.example.com/pricing",
})
// redirect to sess.URL
  • The success URL gets session_id={CHECKOUT_SESSION_ID} appended (Stripe fills it in), unless the URL already has the placeholder, so the page can say thanks.
  • A plan with trialDays starts the trial without asking for a card, and the subscription is canceled at the end if the buyer added none.
  • A subject that already holds a subscription that grants its plan is refused with ErrAlreadySubscribed. Send that subject to the portal instead. The check runs before the session exists, so it stops a second checkout after the first was paid, not two open at once: two tabs with different URLs can both complete. A host that must never bill twice holds a lock per subject around checkout.
  • The same request returns the same session (the idempotency key is derived from the app, subject, plan, interval, price and URLs). Stripe replays a key for a day, so a session that was completed or has expired comes back without a URL; payforge then creates a new one, and a buyer who subscribes, cancels and returns the same day gets a working page.

Paying does not change the account's plan by itself. The plan changes when the subscription's webhook arrives; see the lifecycle.

docs.title: Buying something once
docs.text:
sess, err := client.CheckoutProduct(ctx, payforge.ProductCheckout{
    Subject:     subject,
    Product:     "sample_pack",
    Reference:   "order-8841",
    SuccessURL:  okURL,
    CancelURL:   cancelURL,
})

A fixed-price product is sold at its synced price, and giving an AmountCents is ErrAmountNotAllowed. A seller-set product needs AmountCents at or above the product's minimum (ErrBelowMinimum). Set Reference to your own order ID: retrying with the same reference returns the same session, so a double click does not make two.

docs.title: The customer portal
docs.text:
url, err := client.Portal(ctx, customerID, "https://app.example.com/billing")

The portal is where a buyer updates a card, changes plan and cancels. Configure which of those it allows in the Stripe dashboard. Changes made there come back as subscription events.

docs.title: Mapping errors to responses
docs.text:
Error Meaning Suggested response ErrNotConfigured Free mode 404 or hide the billing UI ErrInvalidSubject, ErrInvalidURL Bad input from your code 400 or 500 ErrUnknownPlan, ErrUnknownProduct Not in the spec 404 ErrNotSelfServe, ErrNoPrice Cannot be bought here 400 ErrBelowMinimum, ErrAmountNotAllowed Bad amount 400 ErrAlreadySubscribed Already subscribed 409, send to the portal ErrNotSynced The catalog was not synced to this account 500, and run sync

Test with errors.Is. Any other error is Stripe's, wrapped with what was attempted.

docs.title: The lifecycle
docs.text:
payforge.Lifecycle turns a verified event into what your code should do. For subscriptions it computes the account's entitlement: which plan it is on now.

life := &payforge.Lifecycle{
    Spec:     spec,
    Store:    store,  // yours
    Sink:     sink,   // yours
    Provider: client, // the Stripe client; reads subscriptions
}
res, err := life.Handle(ctx, ev)

Handle returns an error only when a retry could fix it: the store, the provider or the sink failed. Answer that with a 5xx so Stripe redelivers. Anything else is a 2xx, and res.Outcome says what happened:

Outcome Meaning OutcomeApplied A sink was told OutcomeDuplicate Already processed; nothing changed OutcomeIgnored Not an event the lifecycle acts on, or no sink for it OutcomeSkipped Relevant but cannot be acted on, such as another app's event, a malformed event, or one from a connected account. Reason says why; log it

An event for a customer no account is known for is skipped too, but is not recorded as seen. Stripe often delivers the webhook before your checkout return page has linked the customer to the account; when Stripe redelivers the event after you have, it applies. An event with no ID is an error, because the ID is what lets an event be processed once.

An event is recorded as seen only after the sink applied it. A failed attempt is therefore retried, and a repeated one does nothing.

docs.title: Subscriptions are decided from Stripe, not from the event
docs.text:
After any subscription event the lifecycle lists the customer's subscriptions from Stripe (that is Provider) and picks the highest plan that grants, the later period end breaking a tie. The order events arrive in therefore does not matter:

  • A late "active" for a subscription that has since ended cannot grant the plan.
  • A late "deleted" for an old subscription cannot drop an account that has a new one.

This costs one Stripe API call per subscription event. Serialize per account: Handle does not lock, so two events for the same account handled at the same time can apply in either order, and the later Apply may carry the older state. Hold a lock per Subject (one handler at a time per account is enough), or give your sink a version check. Set Provider in production. Without it the event alone decides, an ended subscription never grants whatever status it carries, and an out-of-order event can leave a stale plan.

docs.title: What grants a plan
docs.text:
• A subscription grants while it is active, trialing or past_due. Past due still grants because Stripe is retrying the payment and cutting access during the retries punishes a customer whose card is being fixed. Every other status, including one this library does not know, does not grant (payforge.Grants).
  • Only a price the spec has can grant. The price's lookup key must name this app, a plan in the spec and an interval that plan prices. A price made by hand in the dashboard with the key taskboard/enterprise/month does not give anyone the arranged Enterprise plan. A subscription from before payforge, with no lookup key, is named by its metadata and counts only for a self-serve plan; a price that has some other lookup key names nothing, whatever the metadata says.
  • With several lines or subscriptions, the highest tier wins; two plans in the same tier resolve by plan ID, so the order of the lines never matters.
  • Events from a seller's own Stripe account are never acted on for subscriptions or refunds. A seller controls the objects in their own account, metadata and prices included, and their events arrive on the same handler as yours (that is why both secrets are configured). Only account.updated is taken from a connected account.
  • With nothing that grants, the account is on the spec's default plan.

docs.title: The ports
docs.text:
You supply two, and optionally more for marketplaces.

type Store interface {
    SubjectForCustomer(ctx context.Context, customerID string) (string, error) // ErrNotFound if none
    Seen(ctx context.Context, eventID string) (bool, error)
    MarkSeen(ctx context.Context, eventID string) error
}

type EntitlementSink interface {
    Apply(ctx context.Context, e payforge.Entitlement) error
}

Store remembers which events were processed, and maps a Stripe customer to your account for events that do not name one. Usually the event names the account in its metadata and the mapping is never used.

Sink updates your own record of the account's plan. Three rules:

  1. Set, do not change. Apply receives the account's whole current entitlement, not a difference. Applying the same one twice must leave the same state.
  2. It will be called more than once for the same event if an earlier attempt failed after it ran.
  3. Do not reject a drop. An entitlement with Granted: false means the account is back on the default plan.

An Entitlement carries Subject, Plan, Granted, SubscribedPlan, Status, ValidUntil (information; the status decides), SubscriptionID, CustomerID, Origin and EventID. Origin lets a host that also sets plans by hand tell where a change came from.

docs.title: Checking your own implementations
docs.text:
Write your store and sink against your database, then run the conformance suites against them in your tests:

func TestStoreConforms(t *testing.T) {
    payforgetest.Store(t, func(t *testing.T) (payforge.Store, func(customerID, subject string)) {
        s := newPostgresStore(t) // fresh and empty
        return s, s.LinkCustomer
    })
}

func TestSinkConforms(t *testing.T) {
    payforgetest.Sink(t, func(t *testing.T) (payforge.EntitlementSink, func(subject string) (payforge.Entitlement, bool)) {
        s := newPostgresSink(t)
        return s, s.Get
    })
}

They check replay safety, concurrent use, unknown customers, whole-state replacement and independent accounts. MemoryStore and MemorySink pass them and are fine for tests and for a host that does not need to survive a restart.

docs.title: Putting it together
docs.text: examples/webhook is the whole path: a handler that verifies, calls Handle, and chooses the status code. Its test drives it with a signed request and shows a redelivery applying once.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text: What payforge does not do, and what has not been proven.

docs.title: Not yet run against real Stripe
docs.text:
Every test uses a stand-in for the Stripe API or hand-written payloads. The stand-in enforces idempotency keys as Stripe documents them, but it is still our reading of Stripe. These have not been confirmed against Stripe's test mode:

  • That a key reused with different parameters is refused, and a key replays its response for a day.
  • The shape of a deleted product when read, and that active is false for it.
  • That Checkout accepts on_behalf_of with a platform-owned customer, and refuses an application fee larger than the amount.
  • Real event payloads under an account's pinned API version, for subscriptions, invoices, charges and accounts.
  • That a charge from a Checkout payment inherits the payment intent's metadata.
  • That a trial that ends without a card emits customer.subscription.deleted.
  • How long Customer Search lags a creation.
  • That transfer_lookup_key moves a key off an archived price.

An opt-in live test against test mode is on the roadmap and will settle these.

docs.title: Design limits
docs.text:
• No locking. Lifecycle.Handle and checkout do not serialize. Hold a lock per account when events can be handled at once, and per subject around checkout if a second subscription must never be possible. See the lifecycle.
  • One Stripe API call per subscription event, and per sale, to read the provider's current state. That is the price of order not mattering.
  • Cross-border sellers are not supported; see marketplaces.
  • A changed customer email inside a day can create a second customer when Search has not caught up, instead of failing.
  • Plan IDs are permanent. Renaming one creates a new product and leaves the old one; see the catalog.
  • Fixed-price sale fees come from the spec, not from the price Stripe holds.
  • One-time sales being paid and delayed payment methods are the host's to record; only refunds are applied.
  • Keyless legacy prices are trusted through the metadata on the platform's own subscriptions. Anyone who can write that metadata can name a self-serve plan for a subscription with a keyless price.
  • In-memory ports (MemoryStore, MemorySink) grow without bound and lose everything on restart. They are for tests.
  • Stripe only. The core is provider-neutral; there is no second adapter.

docs.title: Marketplaces
docs.text:
A spec with a marketplace section lets your sellers be paid directly, with the platform keeping a fee. Each seller has a Stripe Express account: Stripe hosts the onboarding and holds the seller's identity and bank details.

var connect payforge.Connect = client // *stripe.Client implements it

docs.title: Onboarding a seller
docs.text:
acct, err := connect.CreateAccount(ctx, seller, "US") // store acct on the seller
link, err := connect.OnboardingLink(ctx, acct, refreshURL, returnURL)
// redirect the seller to link
  • CreateAccount makes one account per seller; a repeat returns the same one. Stripe cannot search accounts, so store the ID. The country is the seller's two-letter code and cannot be changed later.
  • An onboarding link is single-use and expires in minutes. Stripe sends the seller to refreshURL when it has expired; that page should call OnboardingLink again.
  • Account(ctx, id) reads the account: ChargesEnabled, PayoutsEnabled, DetailsSubmitted. Returning to returnURL does not mean onboarding finished; check, or wait for the account.updated event.

docs.title: A sale
docs.text:
sess, err := connect.CheckoutSale(ctx, payforge.Sale{
    Buyer:         buyer,
    SellerAccount: acct,
    SellerPlan:    "seller",
    Product:       "listing",
    AmountCents:   2599, // for a seller-set product
    Reference:     "order-8841",
    SuccessURL:    okURL,
    CancelURL:     cancelURL,
})

It is a destination charge made on the seller's behalf: the seller is the merchant on the buyer's statement, the money is transferred to the seller's account, and the platform fee is taken as the application fee.

  • The fee is the seller plan's platformFeeBps when it sets one, otherwise the marketplace's, applied to what the buyer pays and rounded down to a cent. A sale of 499 cents at 8% charges 39 cents, not 40. A fee of zero sends no application fee. payforge.FeeBps and payforge.Fee compute it for a pricing page.
  • A seller who cannot take charges is refused with ErrSellerNotReady before any checkout is made. This reads the account, one API call per sale.
  • An account this app did not create is refused with ErrForeignAccount. The money goes to the account named, so an account ID from a request, or a wrong record, cannot pay another app's seller on the same Stripe account.
  • SellerPlan is trusted. It chooses the fee, so take it from your own record of the seller, never from a request.
  • For a fixed-price product the fee is computed from the spec's amount. Keep the catalog synced, or Stripe refuses a fee larger than a lower price.
  • A spec without a marketplace cannot create accounts or sell (ErrNoMarketplace).
  • The fee is on the amount the seller set. Shipping or tax added at checkout is not part of it.

docs.title: Refunds and account changes
docs.text:
Two more ports receive what happens afterwards. Both are optional; without one, its events are ignored (and not recorded, so you can add it later).

life := &payforge.Lifecycle{
    Spec: spec, Store: store, Sink: sink, Provider: client,
    Sales:    saleSink,   // refunds
    Sellers:  sellerSink, // connected-account changes
    Accounts: client,     // read the account's current state
}

type SaleSink interface {
    ApplyRefund(ctx context.Context, r payforge.SaleRefund) error
}
type SellerSink interface {
    ApplySeller(ctx context.Context, a payforge.SellerAccount) error
}
  • Refunds. SaleRefund names the buyer, seller, product, charge and payment intent (to match the order you recorded) and the total refunded so far. A full refund (Full) means the buyer no longer has access to what was bought; keep the data. The total only grows, so keep the highest you have seen and treat a full refund as permanent: a late event for an earlier partial refund must not reopen the sale. Refunds of a subscription's invoice, or of another app's charge, are skipped.
  • Accounts. SellerAccount is the whole current state. With Accounts set, the lifecycle applies what Stripe says now, not what the event says, so a late event cannot turn charges back on. A seller can lose the ability to sell after onboarding; use ChargesEnabled to decide whether to show their listings. Accounts payforge did not create are skipped.

payforgetest.Sales and payforgetest.Sellers check your implementations, as payforgetest.Store does.

docs.title: Sellers outside your Stripe region
docs.text: CreateAccount requests both the card_payments and transfers capabilities, which is what a sale made on the seller's behalf needs. Stripe supports that for sellers in the platform's own region. Sellers elsewhere are onboarded under a different agreement with transfers only, and a sale on their behalf is not possible as written. Treat cross-border sellers as unsupported.

docs.title: Not covered
docs.text:
• A one-time sale being paid. Record it yourself when your checkout completes (EventCheckoutCompleted with Paid), and match a later refund by payment intent.
  • Delayed payment methods that settle days later.
  • Payouts, disputes and transfer reversals; Stripe handles them and sends events payforge ignores.

docs.title: Webhooks
docs.text:
Stripe tells you what happened by posting events to an endpoint you register in the dashboard. payforge verifies each one and reduces it to a small Event.

hook := stripe.Webhook{Secrets: []string{platformSecret, connectSecret}}
ev, err := hook.Read(r) // r is the *http.Request

A complete handler is examples/webhook.

docs.title: What is checked
docs.text:
• The signature comes first, before any of the body is read. A payload is accepted if any one of the configured secrets verifies it, which is how the platform's endpoint and the connected-account endpoint share a handler.
  • A stale signature is refused (older than five minutes; Tolerance changes it), as is a missing or malformed one.
  • The body is limited to 1 MiB (MaxBytes changes it).
  • A secret is never included in an error.
  • The body is read before the signature is checked, up to the limit, so run the endpoint on a server with read timeouts (http.Server.ReadTimeout, or a ReadHeaderTimeout and a reverse proxy that limits slow bodies).
  • Livemode is not enforced. Do not put a test-mode and a live-mode secret in the same list, or test events will be accepted in production.

docs.title: The two failures
docs.text:
Tell them apart, because they need different answers:

Error Meaning Answer payforge.ErrSignatureInvalid Not from Stripe, or stale 400. A retry cannot fix it payforge.ErrPayloadTooLarge Body over the limit 413 Any other error Stripe signed it but it cannot be read, or no secret is configured 500: it is yours to fix, and Stripe will redeliver

Treating an unreadable event as a bad signature would hide your own bug as an attack.

docs.title: The event
docs.text:
Kind Stripe events Carries EventSubscriptionCreated / Updated / Ended customer.subscription.* Subscription: status, every line item's price and lookup key, period end, trial end EventCheckoutCompleted checkout.session.completed, checkout.session.async_payment_succeeded Checkout: mode, whether Paid, payment intent, amount EventInvoicePaid / Failed invoice.paid, invoice.payment_failed Invoice EventAccountUpdated account.updated AccountState EventRefunded charge.refunded Refund EventIgnored everything else only ID and Type

Every event also has ID, Type, Created, Livemode, and the App, Subject, Plan and Product read from the object's metadata. For a subscription with no metadata, the app and plan come from its price's lookup key. Metadata is a copy of the object's own metadata, so you can read keys of your own.

Only a few stable fields are read, into payforge's own structs, so an endpoint pinned to a different Stripe API version than the library's still works. The period end is read from the subscription or, on newer versions, from its items; when the event gives none it is zero, never invented.

Acknowledge an EventIgnored with a 200 and move on. Stripe retries anything else for days.

docs.title: Registering endpoints
docs.text:
• One endpoint for your own account's events: subscriptions, checkout, invoices, refunds, and account.updated for your sellers' accounts.
  • With a marketplace, a second endpoint for events on connected accounts, with its own secret. Both secrets go in Secrets, and CheckStartup requires both.
  • Use separate secrets for test and live mode, and never log them.

docs.title: Event order and replays
docs.text: Stripe does not deliver events in order and delivers some more than once. Do not make decisions from one event's contents alone; hand it to the lifecycle, which is built for exactly this.
